note: Extracted 13 September 2026 and upgraded 14 September 2026. The clinical-development archetype: almost all human evidence comes from one developer's registered trial programme. The phase 2 obesity trial (SRC-050) and its MASLD substudy (SRC-051) are now read in full. For both phase 2 trials the registry records with posted results (SRC-126, SRC-129), the final protocols (SRC-127, SRC-130) and the statistical analysis plans (SRC-128, SRC-131) are held and read, and are kept as distinct sources because each answers a different question. The phase 1b, phase 2 type 2 diabetes and phase 3 articles (SRC-048, SRC-049, SRC-052) remain at abstract level — FULL TEXT NOT HELD — as do the discovery paper, the body-composition substudy and the post hoc biomarker analysis. Trials, and the differences between documents of one trial, are recorded in data/seed/trials/retatrutide-trials.json. Three practitioner sources sit alongside (SRC-003, SRC-004, SRC-005). Amounts appear only in protocol fields, which are practitioner-view only; claim text, plain-language text, gaps and positions describe dose groups without amounts, because patient payloads must not carry dosing merely because a component does not render it.

compound.shortDescription: A single engineered peptide that activates three hormone receptors at once — GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon. In late-stage trials for obesity and type 2 diabetes, run almost entirely by the company developing it.
compound.simpleSummary:
Retatrutide is an investigational medicine made as one peptide that acts on three hormone receptors the body uses to regulate appetite, blood sugar and energy use. It belongs to the same family as semaglutide and tirzepatide, which act on one and two of those receptors.

**It has been studied in a lot of people.** Published trials have tested it in adults with obesity and in adults with type 2 diabetes, including one completed phase 3 trial. In those trials, people given it lost substantially more weight than people given placebo, and people with type 2 diabetes had larger falls in blood sugar. The most common side effects were stomach and bowel symptoms such as nausea and diarrhoea, more often at higher doses.

**Almost all of that evidence comes from one source.** The company developing retatrutide sponsored every trial with published results found on 13 September 2026, and most were done in the United States. That is normal for a medicine in development, and it is still one programme rather than independent confirmation. Large trials of long-term outcomes, such as heart and kidney events, are registered and have not reported.

**It is not an approved medicine** on the records this index holds, and products sold online under its name are not the product used in trials. A published case report describes a man who became seriously unwell after injecting an online-purchased product sold as retatrutide; what that product contained was never tested.
compound.practitionerSummary: Retatrutide (LY3437943) is a unimolecular triple agonist at the GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors; in vitro its glucagon and GLP-1 receptor activity is described as balanced with greater GIP receptor activity. The first-in-human single-ascending-dose study and a 12-week phase 1b multiple-ascending-dose trial in type 2 diabetes reported dose-proportional pharmacokinetics with a half-life of about six days, supporting once-weekly subcutaneous dosing. Phase 2 trials in obesity (48 weeks) and type 2 diabetes (36 weeks) reported dose-dependent reductions in body weight and HbA1c versus placebo, with dose-related, mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal adverse events that were partly mitigated by lower starting doses, and dose-dependent heart-rate increases that peaked at 24 weeks. A liver-fat substudy in MASLD reported large relative reductions at 24 weeks. The first published phase 3 trial (TRANSCEND-T2D-1: monotherapy in type 2 diabetes, USA, Mexico and India, 40 weeks) reported HbA1c and weight reductions at all three maintenance doses, adverse-event discontinuations of 2–5% and no severe hypoglycaemia. ClinicalTrials.gov lists 34 studies on 13 September 2026, 33 with the developer as lead sponsor, including a cardiovascular and kidney outcomes trial that has not reported. Every published efficacy result is developer-sponsored. Practitioner sources describe schedules that no identified trial used, including three-times-weekly administration and 8-weeks-on, 8-weeks-off cycling. For both phase 2 trials this index holds the registry records with posted results, the final protocols and the statistical analysis plans alongside the articles; the obesity trial and its MASLD substudy are read in full, the others at abstract level.
compound.unknownsSummary: Not established: any long-term clinical outcome (cardiovascular, kidney, mortality), since the outcomes trial has not reported; replication by anyone other than the developer; what happens to weight and metabolic measures after stopping, and whether on/off cycling as described by practitioner sources does anything; any schedule other than once weekly; effects in type 1 diabetes, where one case report of an unanalysed online product is the only human record; the composition of products sold outside trials; and head-to-head comparison with tirzepatide, which is registered and has not reported.

aliases.note: The developer's research code. Early publications use it alone; later ones give both names. Same molecule.

compound.molecularDescription: A single synthetic peptide with agonist activity at the GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. The developer's trial protocols describe a linear peptide of 39 amino-acid residues conjugated to a C20 fatty acid moiety, and the obesity trial report describes the conjugate as a fatty diacid moiety. No held document states the sequence, so none is recorded here.
compound.nomenclatureNote: No naming conflict in the scientific record: LY3437943 and retatrutide denote the same molecule. The practical naming problem is elsewhere — products sold online under the name retatrutide are not the trial product, and nothing in the held records establishes what they contain.

claims.claimText: Retatrutide (LY3437943) is a single synthetic peptide — described in the developer's trial protocols as a 39-residue linear peptide conjugated to a C20 fatty acid moiety — with agonist activity at the glucagon, GIP and GLP-1 receptors; relative to the endogenous ligands it is reported as less potent at the human glucagon and GLP-1 receptors and more potent at the GIP receptor, and in obese mice it reduced body weight, with glucagon-receptor-mediated increases in energy expenditure adding to intake reduction.
claims.plainLanguageText: Retatrutide is one engineered peptide that switches on three hormone receptors involved in appetite, blood sugar and energy use.
claims.interpretationNotes: The receptor profile is laboratory pharmacology from the developer's discovery paper, restated with potency ratios in the obesity trial report; the energy-expenditure mechanism is from mice. The structural description comes from the developer's own protocols. None of it is a human measurement.
claims.uncertaintyText: No held document states the amino-acid sequence. How the three receptor activities contribute in people is inferred from this profile and from trial outcomes, not measured directly.

evidence.interpretation: Receptor activity profile in vitro.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Body weight, glycaemic control and energy expenditure in obese mice.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: The sponsor's protocol synopsis describes the molecule as a linear peptide of 39 amino-acid residues conjugated to a C20 fatty acid moiety.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's own trial document as posted to the registry, read in full. It states what was planned; it is not a report of what was done.

evidence.interpretation: The trial report states that, compared with the endogenous ligands, retatrutide is less potent at the human glucagon and GLP-1 receptors (by factors of 0.3 and 0.4) and more potent at the GIP receptor (by a factor of 8.9), citing the discovery paper.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The trial report restates laboratory potency ratios and cites the discovery paper for them; that paper is held at abstract level only, so the ratios have not been traced to the experiment.

claims.claimText: In a phase 1b multiple-ascending-dose trial in type 2 diabetes, retatrutide's pharmacokinetics were dose proportional with a half-life of about six days, and the first-in-human single-dose study reported a pharmacokinetic profile supporting once-weekly dosing.
claims.plainLanguageText: It lasts about six days in the body, which is why trials give it once a week.
claims.interpretationNotes: Two developer studies agree on the once-weekly rationale. The half-life figure is from the phase 1b abstract.
claims.uncertaintyText: Measured in the trial formulation given by subcutaneous injection. Says nothing about other schedules or about products sold outside trials.

evidence.interpretation: Dose-proportional pharmacokinetics, half-life approximately six days, suitability for once-weekly dosing.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Single-ascending-dose phase 1 pharmacokinetics supporting once-weekly dosing.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: In a 48-week phase 2 trial in 338 adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, least-squares mean body-weight change at the 24-week primary endpoint ranged from −7.2% in the lowest-dose group to −17.9% in the highest-responding group against −1.6% with placebo, and at 48 weeks from −8.7% to −24.2% against −2.1%; 2% of placebo participants and 16–83% across retatrutide groups lost 15% or more of their body weight.
claims.plainLanguageText: In a year-long trial in adults with obesity, people on retatrutide lost much more weight than people on placebo, and more at higher doses.
claims.interpretationNotes: Randomised, placebo-controlled and now read in full. The estimate is the efficacy estimand — the effect if treatment had been taken as intended — with no adjustment for multiplicity, a surrogate endpoint (weight), US sites only, and a trial designed, monitored and analysed by the developer. The article, the registry's posted results and the plan agree on design and on every 48-week value; four 24-week group values differ slightly between article and registry, which is recorded against the trial rather than resolved.
claims.uncertaintyText: 48 weeks, 338 participants; the authors read the weight curves as not yet having plateaued. Durability after stopping, and effects on clinical events, are not addressed.

evidence.interpretation: Percentage change in body weight at 24 and 48 weeks by dose group versus placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). The abstract's figures match Table 2.

evidence.interpretation: Table 2: least-squares mean percentage change in body weight at 24 and 48 weeks by group, differences from placebo, and proportions reaching 5%, 10% and 15% reductions.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). Values read from Table 2.

evidence.interpretation: Posted primary and secondary outcome measures: percent change in body weight at weeks 24 and 48 by group, with mixed-model comparisons against placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's structured results as posted to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, read in full from the committed API snapshot. The registry is itself the primary posting; no secondary characterisation stands between it and this index.

claims.claimText: In adults with type 2 diabetes, HbA1c fell more than with placebo in a 36-week phase 2 trial at all but the lowest dose, and in the 40-week phase 3 TRANSCEND-T2D-1 monotherapy trial at all three maintenance doses, with mean body weight change of about −12% to −15% against about −3% with placebo in phase 3.
claims.plainLanguageText: In people with type 2 diabetes, blood sugar and weight fell more than with placebo, in both a phase 2 and a phase 3 trial.
claims.interpretationNotes: The phase 2 result was repeated in a phase 3 trial with a different population mix and countries (USA, Mexico, India), which is the strongest repetition on this record — within the same developer's programme.
claims.uncertaintyText: HbA1c and weight are surrogate endpoints. Both trials were developer-sponsored.

evidence.interpretation: HbA1c at 24 and 36 weeks and body weight at 36 weeks by dose group versus placebo and dulaglutide.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: HbA1c and body weight at 40 weeks versus placebo; phase 3.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Glucose and HbA1c reductions in the higher-dose cohorts of the 12-week phase 1b study.

evidence.interpretation: Posted primary outcome: least-squares mean change in HbA1c from baseline to 24 weeks by group, with comparisons against placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's structured results as posted to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, read in full from the committed API snapshot. The registry is itself the primary posting; no secondary characterisation stands between it and this index.

evidence.interpretation: Posted secondary outcomes: change in body weight in kilograms at 24 and 36 weeks by group.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's structured results as posted to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, read in full from the committed API snapshot. The registry is itself the primary posting; no secondary characterisation stands between it and this index.

claims.claimText: Across the published trials the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal (nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation), dose-related, mostly mild to moderate, occurring mainly during dose escalation and less often with a lower starting dose. In the 48-week obesity trial, read in full, adverse events led to discontinuation in 6–16% of participants across retatrutide groups and in none on placebo, serious adverse events occurred in 4% of both, and no clinically significant hypoglycaemia was reported; no severe hypoglycaemia was reported in the type 2 diabetes trials, and adverse-event discontinuations were 2–5% in the phase 3 trial.
claims.plainLanguageText: The main side effects in trials were stomach and bowel symptoms, more common at higher doses and while doses were being increased. In the year-long obesity trial, some people stopped because of side effects; nobody on placebo did.
claims.interpretationNotes: Consistent across four trials. The obesity-trial figures now come from its full report; the type 2 diabetes trials remain at abstract level, with the phase 2 trial's serious-adverse-event counts also available from its posted registry results. How fast the dose rises changed tolerability, which matters to anyone comparing trial schedules with practitioner schedules.
claims.uncertaintyText: Trials of up to 48 weeks in selected populations. Rare or long-latency harms are not excluded by trials of this size and length. Adverse-event detail by group for the type 2 diabetes trials is not held beyond the registry's tables.

evidence.interpretation: Gastrointestinal events dose-related and mitigated by lower starting dose; heart-rate increases peaked at 24 weeks.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). The abstract's safety summary matches the Results and Table 3.

evidence.interpretation: Gastrointestinal adverse events by group; no severe hypoglycaemia; no deaths.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events, 2–5% adverse-event discontinuation, no severe hypoglycaemia, two deaths judged unrelated.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Gastrointestinal disorders the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events in phase 1b.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

evidence.interpretation: Safety results: adverse events in 70% of placebo and 73–94% of retatrutide participants; discontinuation for adverse events 6–16% versus none; gastrointestinal events mainly during escalation and partly mitigated by a 2 mg start; 15 serious adverse events in 13 participants, 4% in both groups; one death by drowning judged unrelated by the site investigator.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26).

evidence.interpretation: Table 3: adverse events, serious adverse events, deaths and discontinuations by group.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). Values read from Table 3.

evidence.interpretation: Posted adverse-event tables for the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial: serious adverse events in one to three participants per group and no deaths.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's structured results as posted to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, read in full from the committed API snapshot. The registry is itself the primary posting; no secondary characterisation stands between it and this index.

claims.claimText: In a 98-participant substudy of the phase 2 obesity trial in people with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and at least 10% liver fat, mean relative liver-fat change at 24 weeks ranged from about −43% to −82% across retatrutide groups against +0.3% with placebo; liver fat fell below 5% in 27–86% of retatrutide participants and in none on placebo; reductions were maintained at 48 weeks and tracked weight loss; and mean ALT, AST, FIB-4 and ELF did not change consistently against placebo.
claims.plainLanguageText: In people with fatty liver disease in one trial, liver fat fell sharply alongside weight loss. Blood tests of liver injury and scarring did not change in a consistent way.
claims.interpretationNotes: A substudy of the same trial as RETA-003, not an independent trial, and now read in full. Liver fat is an imaging measure; the liver-injury and fibrosis blood markers the article reports did not move consistently, and there was no biopsy.
claims.uncertaintyText: No liver histology, no enrichment for fibrosis, type 2 diabetes excluded, no multiplicity control, and 48-week MRI missing for 56.1% of participants; the authors call the results hypothesis-generating. Whether this changes fibrosis or clinical liver outcomes is not addressed.

evidence.interpretation: Relative change in liver fat at 24 weeks by dose group versus placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the substudy report read (Nat Med 2024;30:2037-48), including Methods and Extended Data. The abstract's figures match the Results.

evidence.interpretation: Liver-fat change at 24 and 48 weeks by group, estimated treatment differences, and proportions reaching normal liver fat.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the substudy report read (Nat Med 2024;30:2037-48), including Methods and Extended Data.

evidence.interpretation: Biomarkers: K-18 and pro-C3 fell in some groups; mean ALT, AST, FIB-4 and ELF did not change consistently versus placebo; no hepatotoxicity signal.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the substudy report read (Nat Med 2024;30:2037-48), including Methods and Extended Data.

evidence.interpretation: Stated limitations: small substudy, US and majority white, type 2 diabetes excluded, no histology, no enrichment for MASH or fibrosis, no multiplicity control, 48-week MRI missing for 56.1%; results hypothesis-generating.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the substudy report read (Nat Med 2024;30:2037-48), including Methods and Extended Data.

claims.claimText: On 13 September 2026 ClinicalTrials.gov listed 34 registered studies of retatrutide, 33 with the developer as lead sponsor: phase 1 pharmacology studies from 2019, phase 2 trials from 2021, a phase 3 programme from 2023 including a cardiovascular and kidney outcomes trial registered for about 10,000 participants that has not completed, an expanded-access programme, and one phase 2 obesity trial led by a different sponsor.
claims.plainLanguageText: Retatrutide is part way through a large development programme. The biggest trials, on heart and kidney outcomes, have not finished.
claims.interpretationNotes: Registry data describe what was registered and its status, not results. The shape of the programme is itself informative: the evidence record is growing quickly and is concentrated in one sponsor.
claims.uncertaintyText: Registry status is time-sensitive and sponsor-reported. Trials registered only elsewhere are not captured.

evidence.interpretation: Registry search results: phases, start dates, sponsors, statuses and enrolment targets. A trial registry, not a regulator's decision.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: A 2026 case report describes a man with type 1 diabetes who developed severe vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and acute kidney injury shortly after self-administering an online-purchased product marketed as retatrutide, with a concurrent Shigella infection; the authors state causation cannot be established.
claims.plainLanguageText: One published case describes a man with type 1 diabetes who became seriously unwell after injecting a product bought online as retatrutide. He also had a gut infection, and the product was never tested.
claims.interpretationNotes: The only human record of use outside trials. Two things are unknown and both matter: what the product contained, and how much of the illness was the infection.
claims.uncertaintyText: A single case with a confounding infection and an unanalysed product. It is a signal about unsupervised use, not evidence about the trial molecule.

evidence.interpretation: Clinical course, confounding infection, and the authors' statement that causation cannot be established.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: In the 48-week obesity trial heart rate rose with retatrutide in a dose-dependent manner up to 24 weeks and declined thereafter; cardiac arrhythmia events (supraventricular arrhythmias and conduction disorders) were reported in 6% of retatrutide participants and 3% of placebo participants, mild to moderate except one severe prolonged-QT event in a participant also treated with ondansetron. Conference abstracts of the two phase 1 studies report heart-rate increases as well: dose-dependent after single injections in healthy participants, returning to near baseline by day 29, and over 12 weeks in type 2 diabetes within most retatrutide cohorts and with dulaglutide, but not with placebo.
claims.plainLanguageText: Heart rate went up during the first half of the obesity trial and then came down. Short early studies also saw heart rate rise. Heart-rhythm events were uncommon and mostly mild.
claims.interpretationNotes: Read in full from the trial report and its Table 3. The article compares the heart-rate increase with that reported for GLP-1 receptor agonists; that comparison is the authors' and is not tested here.
claims.uncertaintyText: One trial of 48 weeks with 337 treated participants read in full. The phase 1 findings are conference abstracts, qualitative, with no size of change given. Heart-rate results for the phase 2 and phase 3 type 2 diabetes trials are not in any held document or in the registry's posted results.

evidence.interpretation: Heart rate increased dose-dependently up to 24 weeks then declined; arrhythmias mild to moderate except one severe prolonged-QT event in a participant treated with ondansetron.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26).

evidence.interpretation: Table 3 (continued): cardiac arrhythmia events in 19 of 337 retatrutide and 2 of 70 placebo participants.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). Values read from Table 3.

evidence.interpretation: First-in-human single-ascending-dose study in 45 healthy participants: dose-dependent increases in heart rate that returned to near baseline by day 29.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A conference abstract, read in full from the publisher's deposited metadata. It reports the study itself but gives no registry number, no numbers by group for this outcome, and no peer-reviewed methods; the journal page refused access.

evidence.interpretation: Phase 1b multiple-ascending-dose study in 72 people with type 2 diabetes: by week 12, pulse and heart rate increased from baseline within most retatrutide cohorts and with dulaglutide, but not with placebo.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A conference abstract, read in full from the publisher's deposited metadata. It reports the study itself but gives no registry number, no numbers by group for this outcome, and no peer-reviewed methods; the journal page refused access.

claims.claimText: In the 48-week obesity trial the text reports cutaneous hyperaesthesia or skin-sensitivity adverse events in 7% of retatrutide participants and 1% of placebo participants, none severe or serious, none with overt skin findings and none leading to discontinuation; Table 3 lists hyperaesthesia or related events in 20 of 337 retatrutide participants (6%).
claims.plainLanguageText: Some people taking retatrutide reported unusual skin sensitivity. None of these reactions was serious, and nobody stopped because of them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded because it is an adverse event not usually associated with this drug class. The article's text and its table give slightly different percentages, and both are shown.
claims.uncertaintyText: One trial; the underlying cause is not established, and the authors state only that the events did not appear related to the magnitude or rate of weight loss.

evidence.interpretation: Cutaneous hyperaesthesia and skin-sensitivity events in 7% versus 1%; none severe, serious, with overt skin findings or leading to discontinuation.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26).

evidence.interpretation: Table 3 (continued): hyperaesthesia or related adverse event in 20 (6%) retatrutide and 1 (1%) placebo participants.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). The table's 6% differs from the text's 7%; both are recorded.

claims.claimText: In the 48-week obesity trial antidrug antibodies developed during treatment in 31 of 337 retatrutide participants (9%) and in 1 of 70 placebo participants, and hypersensitivity adverse events were reported in 9% and 3%; the article does not report whether antibodies affected response or safety.
claims.plainLanguageText: About one in ten people on retatrutide developed antibodies against it. The trial report does not say whether that made a difference.
claims.interpretationNotes: Immunogenicity is expected for a peptide medicine and is measured in trials for that reason. What matters clinically — whether antibodies neutralise the drug or relate to hypersensitivity — is not reported in the held article.
claims.uncertaintyText: Antibody data were unavailable for ten participants. The relationship between antibodies and pharmacokinetics or safety is planned in the protocols but not reported in any held document.

evidence.interpretation: Table 3 (continued): antidrug antibodies during treatment and hypersensitivity events by group.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26). Values read from Table 3.

claims.claimText: Both phase 2 trials were designed, monitored and analysed by the developer, had no data monitoring committee, applied no adjustment for multiplicity, and took as their primary estimand the effect if treatment had been taken as intended. The type 2 diabetes trial's statistical analysis plan records that three interim analyses were planned after its protocol was approved, the third requested by the developer's senior management to support end-of-phase-2 interactions with regulators; the obesity trial's plan records a third interim analysis added on the same request, although its protocol stated that no interim analyses were planned.
claims.plainLanguageText: Both phase 2 trials were run and analysed by the company developing the drug, and some analyses were added after the trials were planned. The trials' own planning documents say so.
claims.interpretationNotes: Read from the protocols and statistical analysis plans posted to the registry, and from the trial report's own description of the sponsor's role. These are ordinary features of developer-run phase 2 trials and are recorded as context for reading the results, not as a finding that anything was wrong. Adjudication committees for deaths and selected events existed; they are not data monitoring committees.
claims.uncertaintyText: The held protocol and plan versions are final amendments approved after primary completion, so earlier versions cannot be compared. Nothing held shows that any analysis was changed in response to results.

evidence.interpretation: Type 2 diabetes protocol synopsis: 'Data Monitoring Committee: No'.

evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26).

evidence.primaryTraceNote: Full text of the trial report read (N Engl J Med 2023;389:514-26).

claims.claimText: In a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry substudy of the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial (189 enrolled; 103 with baseline and week-36 scans), total fat mass fell by 4.9% in the lowest-dose retatrutide group and by 15.2% to 26.1% in the higher-dose groups, against 4.5% with placebo and 2.6% with dulaglutide; the authors state that the proportion of lean-mass loss to weight loss was similar to other obesity treatments.
claims.plainLanguageText: In people with type 2 diabetes, body scans showed that much of the weight lost on retatrutide was fat. The researchers say the share of muscle and other lean tissue lost was similar to other weight-loss medicines, but the abstract does not give those figures.
claims.interpretationNotes: A substudy of the same trial as the type 2 diabetes results in RETA-004, not a separate trial, and developer-authored. The lean-mass comparison is the authors' statement, not a figure this index can check.
claims.uncertaintyText: Abstract only: lean-mass values are not given, and only 103 of 189 substudy participants had both scans. No body-composition data are held for the obesity trials.

evidence.interpretation: Percent change in total fat mass at week 36 by group versus placebo and dulaglutide, and the authors' statement on the lean-mass proportion.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: A post hoc analysis of both phase 2 trials reports reductions with retatrutide against placebo in non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particles and small LDL particles in both trials, and in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 in the obesity trial only.
claims.plainLanguageText: In a later analysis of the two phase 2 trials, blood fats linked to heart disease fell, and markers of inflammation fell in people without diabetes.
claims.interpretationNotes: Biomarkers are surrogate measures, not cardiovascular events, and the analysis was post hoc and developer-authored. It adds context to the unresolved question of cardiovascular outcomes; it does not answer it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Abstract only; post hoc; false-discovery-rate adjustment as stated in the abstract. Whether these changes translate into fewer cardiovascular events awaits the registered outcomes trial.

evidence.interpretation: Placebo-adjusted percentage changes in lipoprotein and inflammatory biomarkers in the two phase 2 trials.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The cited source is the research itself, held at abstract level: design, setting and size are reliable at this depth and the detail of how outcomes were collected is not.

claims.claimText: The adverse-event tables posted to the registry for the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial list serious adverse events of acute pancreatitis in two participants, atrial fibrillation in one and chronic cholecystitis in one — all in retatrutide groups, none in the placebo or dulaglutide groups. Among events above the 5% reporting threshold, nausea, diarrhoea and decreased appetite were listed more often in the higher maintenance-dose retatrutide groups than in the lowest-dose group or with placebo; vomiting and constipation are also listed, without a consistent pattern across groups.
claims.plainLanguageText: In the diabetes trial's own posted results, a few serious events such as inflammation of the pancreas and an irregular heart rhythm occurred in people taking retatrutide. Nausea, diarrhoea and loss of appetite were among the side effects listed most often.
claims.interpretationNotes: Read from the sponsor's posted registry results because the trial article is held at abstract level only. Single serious events in groups of 23 to 47 participants cannot establish a rate or a cause, and the posting does not say whether investigators judged them related.
claims.uncertaintyText: Non-serious events appear in the posting only above a 5% threshold, so a term's absence there is not evidence it did not occur. No heart-rate measurements or adverse events of special interest are posted; those remain a question for the article's full text.

evidence.interpretation: Serious adverse events by term and group, and other adverse events above the 5% threshold by term and group, as posted.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The sponsor's structured results as posted to the ClinicalTrials.gov record, read in full from the committed API snapshot. The registry is itself the primary posting; no secondary characterisation stands between it and this index.

notYetSupported.statement: Any effect of retatrutide on cardiovascular events, kidney outcomes or mortality.
notYetSupported.why: The outcomes trial is registered and had not completed on the search date. Every published efficacy result is on surrogate measures.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Results of the registered cardiovascular and kidney outcomes trial.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does retatrutide change the rate of cardiovascular and kidney events compared with placebo in people at elevated risk?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. The phase 2 registry results, protocols and plans, and a post hoc lipoprotein and inflammation analysis, were added; biomarkers are surrogate measures and the outcomes trial has not reported.

notYetSupported.statement: Replication of the efficacy findings by anyone other than the developer.
notYetSupported.why: Every trial with published outcomes identified in the screen was sponsored by or affiliated with the developer.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: An independently funded trial or pooled analysis with access to participant-level data.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Do independent investigators, with no developer funding, reproduce the weight and glycaemic effects reported in the developer's trials?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. Every document added in this upgrade — publications, registry postings, protocols and plans — is authored, posted or funded by the developer.

notYetSupported.statement: Any schedule other than once-weekly administration, including three-times-weekly use described by a practitioner source.
notYetSupported.why: Every identified human study used once-weekly subcutaneous dosing, consistent with a half-life of about six days.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A pharmacokinetic and tolerability study of a non-weekly schedule.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: Does splitting weekly exposure into more frequent administrations change pharmacokinetics or gastrointestinal tolerability?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. Both phase 2 protocols specify once-weekly administration only; no held document studies another schedule.

notYetSupported.statement: What happens after stopping, and whether on/off cycling as described by practitioner sources has any effect.
notYetSupported.why: No identified trial tested cycling. A maintenance trial is registered and had not reported in the screened literature.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Results of the registered weight-maintenance trial, or a randomised withdrawal study.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: How much of the weight and metabolic change persists after stopping, and does intermittent treatment preserve it?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. The posted results cover the treatment period plus a four-week safety follow-up; no held document reports weight or metabolic measures after stopping.

notYetSupported.statement: What products sold outside trials under the name retatrutide actually contain.
notYetSupported.why: The one human case involving such a product did not analyse it. A letter on composition and labelling of products sold in Australia was identified by title but has no abstract, so its findings are not recorded.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Analytical characterisation of purchased products against a reference standard, reported in full.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What is the identity, content and purity of products sold online as retatrutide, compared with the declared label?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. Nothing in the new documents concerns products sold outside trials.

notYetSupported.statement: Safety or effect in type 1 diabetes.
notYetSupported.why: No trial identified included people with type 1 diabetes. The only record is one case report of an unanalysed online product with a confounding infection.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A controlled study in type 1 diabetes, or systematic adverse-event reporting that identifies the product.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What are the risks of ketosis and hypoglycaemia when a glucagon-receptor-active incretin agonist is used by people with type 1 diabetes?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. The registered eligibility criteria of both phase 2 trials exclude type 1 diabetes.

notYetSupported.statement: How much of the weight lost is fat rather than lean tissue, in people.
notYetSupported.why: A practitioner source describes the loss as almost entirely body fat on the strength of a mouse study figure. A body-composition substudy in type 2 diabetes exists; its results were not extracted into this record.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Extraction of the DXA substudy results, and body-composition data from the phase 3 trials.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: What proportion of retatrutide-associated weight loss is lean mass, and does it differ from other incretin therapies?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. A body-composition substudy of the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial (SRC-132, abstract) reports fat-mass reductions by group and states that the lean-mass share of weight lost was similar to other obesity treatments. Lean-mass values need the full text, and no body-composition data are held for the obesity trials.

notYetSupported.statement: How retatrutide compares directly with tirzepatide or semaglutide.
notYetSupported.why: Comparisons in the literature and in practitioner sources are across different trials. A head-to-head trial against tirzepatide and one against semaglutide are registered and had not reported.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Results of the registered head-to-head trials.
notYetSupported.researchQuestion: In a randomised head-to-head trial, how do weight, glycaemic and tolerability outcomes compare between retatrutide and tirzepatide?

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026. No head-to-head result is in any held document.

notYetSupported.statement: Group-level safety detail for the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial beyond the registry's adverse-event tables: heart rate, adverse events of special interest, and discontinuations for adverse events by group.
notYetSupported.why: The article (Rosenstock et al., Lancet 2023) is held at abstract level. The registry posts serious and other adverse events and reasons for leaving the study, but not heart rate or adverse events of special interest; the protocol and plan show these were planned.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The full text and appendix of Rosenstock et al., Lancet 2023 (FULL TEXT NOT HELD).

resolution.note: Checked 14 September 2026 against the trial's wider evidence, since the article's full text is not held. The registry's posted serious events and events above the 5% threshold are now extracted (RETA-015). Heart rate, adverse events of special interest and discontinuations for adverse events by group are not posted anywhere held, so this remains open.

notYetSupported.statement: Adverse events of special interest, heart rate and discontinuation detail for the phase 3 TRANSCEND-T2D-1 trial.
notYetSupported.why: The article (Bajaj et al., Lancet 2026) is held at abstract level and the registry record has no posted results.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The full text of Bajaj et al., Lancet 2026 (FULL TEXT NOT HELD), or results posted to NCT06354660.

notYetSupported.statement: Pharmacokinetic parameters beyond the half-life, and the per-cohort safety detail, of the phase 1b trial.
notYetSupported.why: The article (Urva et al., Lancet 2022) is held at abstract level and NCT04143802 has no posted results.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The full text of Urva et al., Lancet 2022 (FULL TEXT NOT HELD).

notYetSupported.statement: How much lean mass was lost with retatrutide in the type 2 diabetes body-composition substudy.
notYetSupported.why: The abstract gives fat-mass changes and a qualitative statement about lean mass, but no lean-mass values.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The full text of Coskun et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2025.

notYetSupported.statement: Why four 24-week body-weight group values in the obesity trial, and the 24-week placebo HbA1c value in the type 2 diabetes trial, differ slightly between the published articles and the registry's posted results.
notYetSupported.why: Both describe the same outcome and a similar analysis population, and neither explains the difference. The obesity article's Supplementary Appendix, which holds its estimand analyses, was refused to this index by the publisher's site.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The obesity trial's Supplementary Appendix (Tables S4–S5), the full text of Rosenstock et al. 2023, or a statement from the sponsor.

notYetSupported.statement: Whether the first-in-human single-dose study reported in the discovery paper is the study registered as NCT03841630.
notYetSupported.why: The registry record lists no publication and the discovery paper's abstract gives no registry number, so the link is plausible and unconfirmed; the two are not merged.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The full text of Coskun et al., Cell Metab 2022.

routes.populationModel: Adults with obesity or overweight, and adults with type 2 diabetes, in developer-sponsored phase 1 to phase 3 trials.
routes.formulation: The developer's trial formulation, injected once weekly.
routes.pkNotes: Half-life about six days with dose-proportional exposure in phase 1b.
routes.limitationsNotes: The only route studied in people. Evidence for this route is evidence about the trial product on a once-weekly schedule.

pharmacokinetics.doseContext: Repeat once-weekly dosing across five ascending cohorts
pharmacokinetics.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes, four US centres

protocols.objectiveContext: Safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in type 2 diabetes (phase 1b, NCT04143802).
protocols.populationModel: 72 adults with type 2 diabetes at four US centres.
protocols.formulation: Trial formulation, once-weekly injection; placebo and dulaglutide comparators.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A phase 1b trial's dose cohorts, chosen to find tolerable doses. Not a treatment schedule and not an approved dose.
protocols.amountReported: Cohorts of 0.5 mg, 1.5 mg and 3 mg, and stepwise escalations of 3/6 mg and 3/6/9/12 mg
protocols.titrationText: The two highest cohorts reached their top dose by stepwise escalation.
protocols.safetyNotes: Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events.

protocols.objectiveContext: Glycaemic control and body weight in type 2 diabetes (phase 2, NCT04867785).
protocols.populationModel: 281 adults with type 2 diabetes at 42 US centres, on diet and exercise alone or stable metformin.
protocols.formulation: Trial formulation, once-weekly injection; placebo and dulaglutide comparators, double-dummy.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A phase 2 trial's dose-finding arms. Not a treatment schedule and not an approved dose.
protocols.amountReported: Maintenance doses of 0.5 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg or 12 mg
protocols.titrationText: 4 mg reached from a 2 mg start or with no escalation; 8 mg from a 2 mg (slow) or 4 mg (fast) start; 12 mg from a 2 mg start.
protocols.combinationsText: Background diet and exercise, with or without stable metformin.
protocols.safetyNotes: Mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events in 35% across retatrutide groups, from 13% in the lowest-dose group to 50% in the 8 mg fast-escalation group. No severe hypoglycaemia and no deaths.

protocols.objectiveContext: Body weight in obesity or overweight without diabetes (phase 2, NCT04881760).
protocols.populationModel: 338 adults aged 18 to 75 with BMI 30 to 50, or 27 to under 30 with a weight-related condition, without diabetes, at US sites; enrolment managed for approximately equal numbers of women and men.
protocols.formulation: Trial formulation, once-weekly injection; placebo comparator.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A phase 2 trial's dose-finding arms. Not a treatment schedule and not an approved dose.
protocols.titrationText: Groups assigned 4 mg or more started at 2 mg or 4 mg with escalation every 4 weeks for up to 12 weeks: 4 mg from a 2 mg or 4 mg start; 8 mg from a 2 mg or 4 mg start; 12 mg from a 2 mg start.
protocols.monitoringText: A 4-week safety follow-up followed the 48-week treatment period. Eight retatrutide participants whose BMI fell to 22 or lower had protocol-driven dose reductions (p. 520).
protocols.safetyNotes: Adverse events led to discontinuation in 6–16% across retatrutide groups and in no placebo participants. Gastrointestinal events occurred mainly during escalation and were less frequent with a 2 mg than a 4 mg start. Heart rate rose dose-dependently to 24 weeks and declined thereafter.
protocols.combinationsText: All participants received a lifestyle intervention with regular counselling by a dietitian or qualified professional; the protocol did not require a specific energy deficit.

protocols.objectiveContext: Monotherapy in type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled by diet and exercise (phase 3 TRANSCEND-T2D-1, NCT06354660).
protocols.populationModel: 537 adults with type 2 diabetes at 48 sites in the USA, Mexico and India.
protocols.formulation: Trial formulation, once-weekly injection; placebo comparator.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A phase 3 trial's arms. Not an approved dose: no approval is recorded for retatrutide in this index.
protocols.safetyNotes: Mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal events that subsided over time; 2–5% discontinued for adverse events; no severe hypoglycaemia; two deaths in one retatrutide group judged unrelated.

protocols.objectiveContext: Fat loss, as framed by the cheat sheet.
protocols.formulation: 10 mg vial reconstituted with 2 ml bacteriostatic water; 10 units on a 1 ml insulin syringe per dose, as stated by the source; injection route not named.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A practitioner quick-reference schedule for an investigational compound. No identified trial used this frequency or cycling, and it is not an approved dose. The table does not name a route; it is recorded under route other, rather than inferring subcutaneous from a syringe.
protocols.cycleText: 8 weeks on, 8 weeks off (or until goal weight is reached)

protocols.objectiveContext: Obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk reduction, as framed by the guide.
protocols.regulatoryContext: A practitioner guide's description for an investigational compound. The guide cites no study for its amounts, and it is not an approved dose.
protocols.titrationText: Gradual titration based on clinical response and tolerance; higher doses within a structured dose-escalation protocol.
protocols.combinationsText: Listed in a fat-loss stack with MOTS-c, tesamorelin and ipamorelin (file p. 176).
protocols.monitoringText: People with a history of pancreatitis, gallbladder disease or severe gastrointestinal conditions should be monitored closely.
protocols.safetyNotes: Gastrointestinal discomfort, particularly during dose escalation; potential gallbladder issues or pancreatitis as with other GLP-1-based therapies; transient fatigue or dizziness.

disagreements.plainLanguageText: Every trial gave retatrutide once a week. A practitioner cheat sheet lists it three times a week.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The trial schedule rests on a measured half-life of about six days. The cheat sheet gives no reason for its frequency and cites no study. That does not show the cheat sheet is wrong about what anybody does; it shows no identified study examined that schedule.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A pharmacokinetic and tolerability study of a more frequent schedule.

positions.positionText: Once weekly, in every dose group, for 48 weeks.
Pharmacokinetics with a half-life of about six days suggest suitability for once-weekly dosing.
Three times per week, in the morning, 8 weeks on and 8 weeks off.

disagreements.topic: How the phase 1 weight result is reported.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: A practitioner book reports the early trial's weight loss as a plain average. The trial reported it as the difference from placebo in its highest-dose group.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The book's figure matches the trial abstract's largest placebo-adjusted reduction, which came from the smallest, highest-escalation cohort after 12 weeks. Presented without those qualifiers and set beside a 40-week tirzepatide trial, it reads as a like-for-like comparison, which it is not.
disagreements.resolutionBasis: The phase 1b abstract (SRC-048) reports the figure as a placebo-adjusted reduction in the top escalation cohort at 12 weeks. The book gives the same number without either qualifier.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: None further: the primary abstract states the conditions.

positions.positionText: Placebo-adjusted body-weight reduction appeared dose dependent, largest in the highest stepwise-escalation cohort at week 12.
Describes the phase 1 result as a mean body weight loss after 12 weeks and compares it with a tirzepatide phase 3 result at 40 weeks.

disagreements.topic: Whether the weight lost is almost all fat.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: A practitioner book says most of the weight lost is pure body fat. The figure it points to is from mice.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The book presents a mouse study comparison figure and draws a body-composition conclusion in the same passage about human use. Human body composition has since been reported at abstract level for the type 2 diabetes trial: fat mass fell substantially, and the authors state that the lean-mass share of weight lost was similar to other obesity treatments, which does not fit 'almost entirely fat'. Without the lean-mass values the human answer is recorded as partly characterised rather than settled.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: Lean-mass values from the full text of the body-composition substudy (SRC-132), and body-composition data from the obesity trials.

positions.positionText: Points to an early preclinical study in mice as showing larger weight loss than tirzepatide.
States that most of the weight loss is pure body fat.
Reports body-weight reduction and energy-expenditure effects in obese mice; the abstract makes no human body-composition statement.
In people with type 2 diabetes, scans showed substantial fat-mass loss, and the authors state that the lean-mass proportion of weight lost was similar to other obesity treatments.

regulatory.indicationContext: Obesity, type 2 diabetes and related conditions
regulatory.authority: No regulator's own record has been consulted for this compound
regulatory.notes: Recorded as investigational on the strength of the registered phase 3 programme and an expanded-access registration, which describe a medicine in development. A trial registry is not a regulator: no authority's own approval, authorisation or refusal has been read, and none is recorded here. Sale of products under this name outside trials is not evidence of any regulatory status.

identities.chemicalForm: Single synthetic peptide, GIP/GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist
identities.usageContext: Developer trial reports use the name and the research code together for the trial product.
identities.notes: No held document states the sequence. The developer's protocols describe 39 residues conjugated to a C20 fatty acid moiety.

identities.usageContext: A case report of self-administration outside healthcare; the product was not analysed.
identities.notes: Recorded separately so that nothing about the trial product is read as describing this product, or the reverse.

identities.usageContext: A practitioner cheat sheet lists vial contents and a schedule under the name, with no manufacturer or characterisation.

replication.finding: Retatrutide reduced body weight more than placebo.
replication.models: Adults with obesity or overweight; adults with type 2 diabetes.
replication.basis: Phase 1b (USA), two phase 2 trials (USA) and one phase 3 trial (USA, Mexico, India), in different populations and durations, all sponsored by or affiliated with the developer. Repeated across trials and countries; not replicated by an independent group. Counted by trial, not by publication: the MASLD, body-composition and biomarker papers share participants with these trials and add none.
replication.limitations: One programme. Surrogate endpoint. Up to 48 weeks.

replication.finding: Retatrutide lowered HbA1c more than placebo in type 2 diabetes.
replication.basis: Phase 1b and phase 2 in the USA, phase 3 in the USA, Mexico and India; all developer-sponsored. Counted by trial, not by publication: the MASLD, body-composition and biomarker papers share participants with these trials and add none.

replication.finding: Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, and more frequent at higher doses or faster escalation.
replication.models: Adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes.
replication.basis: Reported in each of the four trial abstracts; the starting-dose effect is stated in the obesity trial and visible by group in the type 2 diabetes trial. Counted by trial, not by publication: the MASLD, body-composition and biomarker papers share participants with these trials and add none.
replication.limitations: Adverse-event reporting in abstracts is summary-level.

replication.finding: Retatrutide reduced liver fat in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
replication.basis: One substudy of the phase 2 obesity trial, read in full.
replication.limitations: Imaging endpoint; substudy of a larger trial.

replication.models: Healthy participants (single dose) and adults with type 2 diabetes (repeat dose).
replication.basis: The first-in-human single-dose study and the phase 1b repeat-dose trial, both developer-run.

replication.finding: Effects and harms of products sold outside trials under the name.
replication.basis: One case report with an unanalysed product and a confounding infection. There is nothing to replicate yet.
